Fix: reference Redis by its compose service name (e.g. redis:6379), since compose provides DNS resolution between services on the shared network. Ensure both services are on the same network and the Redis port is exposed to other containers.

questions.question: A developer says their two Docker containers on a custom bridge network can't reach each other by container name, even though both are on the same network. Pinging by container name fails with 'unknown host'. How would you diagnose and fix this?
questions.answer: Verify both containers are actually on the same user-defined network with 'docker network inspect <net>' (default 'bridge' has no automatic DNS; user-defined networks do). Ensure you used --network or a shared network in compose, and reference containers by their service/container name, not localhost. Recreate containers attached to the same user-defined bridge so Docker's embedded DNS resolves names.

questions.question: During an incident an on-call asks you to quickly find which container on a busy Docker host is generating the most log output and filling the disk, without stopping any containers. How would you approach this?
questions.answer: Check per-container log sizes under /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log with du -sh to find the biggest. Map the container ID to a name via docker ps. Tail the noisy container with docker logs --tail 50 -f <id> to see what's spamming. Short-term: truncate the log file or configure log rotation (max-size, max-file) in the daemon or compose. Address the root cause of excessive logging in the app.

questions.question: A teammate reports that after a recent deploy your Nginx-based Docker container returns a 502 Bad Gateway for all requests, even though the upstream app container is running and you can curl the app directly from your laptop. Both containers run on the same host under docker-compose. How would you diagnose and fix the 502?
questions.answer: Check whether Nginx can reach the app by container name over the compose network, not localhost. Exec into the Nginx container and curl http://app:port. A 502 usually means Nginx can't reach the upstream — verify the upstream host/port in nginx.conf matches the app's service name and internal port (not the published one), confirm both are on the same compose network, and check depends_on/startup order. Fix the upstream address and reload N…

questions.question: A developer says their Docker build fails on the CI runner with 'no space left on device', though the same build works on their laptop. The runner has been building images for weeks. How would you diagnose and fix this?
questions.answer: Run docker system df to see space used by images, containers, volumes, and build cache — dangling layers and old images accumulate over time. Free space with docker system prune -af --volumes (careful with volumes) or docker builder prune. Check host disk with df -h. Long-term, add a scheduled prune to the runner or use a cleanup step in the pipeline and monitor disk usage.

questions.question: A developer says their Docker container works locally but on the production host it starts as root, and the security team flagged that the app process runs as root inside the container. The Dockerfile has no USER instruction. How would you fix this so the app runs as a non-root user?
questions.answer: By default containers run as root when no USER is set. Add a non-root user in the Dockerfile: create it (e.g. RUN adduser -D appuser), set ownership of needed files with chown, then add USER appuser before the CMD. Ensure the app doesn't need privileged ports (<1024) or adjust to a higher port. Rebuild, and verify with docker exec <c> whoami. Optionally enforce via securityContext runAsNonRoot in Kubernetes.

questions.question: Your Docker image build is extremely slow and the final image is over 1.5GB for a small Python app. Every code change forces a full reinstall of dependencies. How would you reduce build time and image size?
questions.answer: Order Dockerfile steps so dependencies install before copying app code, so dependency layers stay cached when only code changes. Use a slim base image (e.g., python:3.x-slim) and a multi-stage build to exclude build tools from the final image. Add a .dockerignore to skip unnecessary files. Combine RUN steps and clean package caches. This leverages layer caching and shrinks the final image.

questions.question: Your team wants to run the same container image across dev, staging, and prod, but developers keep hardcoding environment-specific config (DB URLs, feature flags) into the image, forcing a rebuild per environment. How would you fix this so one image works everywhere?
questions.answer: Externalize config from the image. Inject settings at runtime via environment variables, ConfigMaps/Secrets in Kubernetes, or mounted config files. The image should stay immutable; only the config layer changes per environment. This follows the 12-factor 'config in environment' principle, enabling build-once-deploy-anywhere and faster, consistent releases.

questions.question: Your Docker Compose setup for local development has a database container and an app container, but the app intermittently fails on startup with 'connection refused' to the DB. The DB container is defined and starts, but the app sometimes races ahead. How would you fix this reliably?
questions.answer: depends_on only waits for container start, not DB readiness. Add a healthcheck to the DB service and use depends_on with condition: service_healthy. Alternatively add retry/backoff logic or a wait-for-it/wait-for-port script in the app's entrypoint. The app should tolerate the DB being temporarily unavailable rather than assuming instant availability.

questions.question: As a junior engineer, you notice a Docker image being built in your pipeline takes 15 minutes because 'pip install' runs every time, even for minor CSS changes. How do you optimize this?
questions.answer: Implement Docker multi-stage builds and leverage layer caching. Copy only the requirements.txt file first and run 'pip install' before copying the rest of your application code. This ensures the dependency installation layer is only rebuilt when the requirements.txt file changes, significantly speeding up subsequent builds for code-only updates.

questions.question: A container in your local Docker environment fails to resolve external hostnames, but the host machine has no issues with DNS. What steps would you take to troubleshoot the container's networking?
questions.answer: I would first check the container's '/etc/resolv.conf' to see if it is pointing to a valid DNS resolver. I would then verify if the Docker daemon is correctly inheriting the host's DNS settings or if a custom '--dns' flag is required. I would test connectivity from within the container using 'nslookup' or 'dig' to identify if the issue is DNS resolution or overall network connectivity to the upstream gateway.

questions.question: A Docker container is crashing on startup. You suspect it's failing to connect to a mandatory environment variable-based secret, but the container exits so fast you can't inspect it. How do you troubleshoot the startup command without modifying the Dockerfile?
questions.answer: Override the entrypoint during runtime using 'docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it <image_name>'. This keeps the container alive in an interactive shell, allowing you to manually inspect environment variables with 'env', test connectivity, and run the start command manually to observe the exact error message.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline uses a Multi-Stage Dockerfile to build an application. You notice the final image is still very large, containing build tools like gcc and maven. How do you modify your Dockerfile to exclude these from the final production image?
questions.answer: Use a multi-stage build. In the first stage, use a base image with necessary build tools to compile the artifact. In the final stage, use a 'FROM' command with a smaller, runtime-only image (like alpine or distroless), and use the 'COPY --from=<stage_name>' command to copy only the compiled binary or JAR file from the builder stage into the final image.

questions.question: A containerized application is throwing 'Connection Refused' when trying to reach an external API. The host machine can ping the API fine. How do you troubleshoot the container networking?
questions.answer: First, inspect the container's /etc/resolv.conf to check DNS configuration. Then, use 'docker run --rm busybox nslookup <hostname>' inside the network namespace to see if the container can resolve the domain. If it can resolve but not connect, check if the Docker network bridge has restricted outbound access via iptables or if the host's firewall (ufw/firewalld) is blocking the container's subnet traffic.

questions.question: Notice a Docker container is failing to mount a host volume, resulting in an 'access denied' error. The host directory exists and has global read/write permissions. How do you investigate this?
questions.answer: Check for SELinux or AppArmor constraints. These security modules often restrict container access to host files even if standard Linux permissions allow it. Run 'dmesg | grep -i denied' or check system audit logs to confirm if an AVC (Access Vector Cache) denial is occurring, then adjust the context with 'z' or 'Z' flags in the docker run volume mount if applicable.

questions.question: A Docker container using a bind mount to a host directory is failing with 'Permission Denied'. How do you verify the mismatch between the container's user ID and the host file ownership?
questions.answer: First, use 'docker exec -it <container_id> id' to check the effective UID inside the container. Then, run 'ls -n <host_path>' on the host to see the numeric UID/GID of the files. If they don't match, the container process lacks permissions. You can resolve this by adjusting file ownership on the host to match the container's user, or by running the container with the '--user' flag set to the host's UID.

questions.question: A Jenkins CI pipeline fails because a Docker image build hangs. You suspect a stale process is locking the Docker socket. How do you safely find and clean up only the stuck build process?
questions.answer: Run 'docker ps' to see if any containers are stuck in 'Created' or 'Running' state for an abnormal duration. Use 'ps aux | grep docker' to identify the specific process ID (PID) of the build or container runtime task. Avoid 'docker system prune' as it affects all containers. Instead, use 'docker stop <container_id>' on the specific ID. If unresponsive, check the Docker daemon logs via 'journalctl -u docker' for hardware or resource saturation …

questions.question: You suspect a Docker container is not respecting its CPU limits. The container is running a heavy calculation. How do you verify the actual CPU shares the container is receiving compared to the allocated quota?
questions.answer: Use 'docker stats' to monitor real-time resource consumption. To verify the settings, inspect the container configuration using 'docker inspect <container_id>'. Look under 'HostConfig.CpuShares' or 'HostConfig.NanoCpus'. Compare these values against the host's performance metrics using 'top' or 'htop' to see if the process is hitting the kernel-enforced throttling limits.

questions.question: A local Docker container using an entrypoint script fails immediately after startup. How do you inspect the exit code and logs without the container disappearing?
questions.answer: Run the container with '--rm=false' (or don't use --rm). Once it exits, use 'docker ps -a' to see the exit status code. Run 'docker inspect <container_id>' to see the state, and use 'docker logs <container_id>' to retrieve the stdout/stderr output generated by the entrypoint script during the crash.

questions.question: A junior engineer notices that a Docker container running a web server is reporting 'Connection Refused' when accessed from the host machine, even though the process is running. How do you verify the container's port binding configuration?
questions.answer: Use 'docker ps' to check the 'PORTS' column to ensure the host port is correctly mapped to the container port (e.g., 8080:80). If the mapping looks correct, use 'docker inspect <container-id>' to check the 'Config.ExposedPorts'. Finally, use 'netstat -tulpn' or 'ss -tulpn' on the host to confirm the Docker daemon is actually listening on the mapped host port. If not, the application inside the container might be bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0…

questions.question: Your Docker container runs a Python web app, but when you try to view logs with 'docker logs <container>' after the app writes to a log file inside the container, you see nothing — the logs command returns empty even though the app is clearly processing requests. Why, and how should the app be configured so logs show up?
questions.answer: The app writes to a file inside the container, but 'docker logs' only captures stdout/stderr. Fix: configure the app to log to stdout/stderr (console handler) instead of a file, following the 12-factor logging approach. Then Docker's logging driver captures output and 'docker logs' works. For files, you'd otherwise need to exec in and cat the file or mount a volume.

questions.question: A developer wants to run their app container on a specific port so it's reachable from the host at http://localhost:9000/, but the app inside the container listens on port 8080. They ran 'docker run myapp' and can't reach it from the host at all. How would you make the app reachable at localhost:9000?
questions.answer: The container port isn't published to the host. Use 'docker run -p 9000:8080 myapp' — the left side (9000) is the host port, the right side (8080) is the container port the app listens on. Verify the app binds to 0.0.0.0 not 127.0.0.1 inside the container, then confirm with 'docker ps' showing the port mapping and curl localhost:9000.

questions.question: A developer wants to share persistent data between two containers running on the same Docker host so both can read and write the same files. Right now each container has its own copy and changes aren't seen by the other. How would you set this up?
questions.answer: Use a shared Docker volume mounted into both containers. Create it with 'docker volume create shared-data', then run both containers with '-v shared-data:/path/in/container'. Both will read/write the same underlying storage. For files on the host, use a bind mount '-v /host/path:/container/path'. In Compose, define the volume once and reference it in both services under volumes.

questions.question: After migrating an app to Docker, containers on a busy host randomly fail to start with 'no space left on device', yet df -h on the root filesystem shows plenty of free space. How would you diagnose and resolve this?
questions.answer: Check docker system df and df -i — the issue is often inode exhaustion or Docker's overlay/volumes dir filling a separate mount. Dangling images, stopped containers, unused volumes and build cache accumulate. Run docker system prune -a --volumes (carefully), clean old images, and set up log rotation / a cron cleanup to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: A colleague reports that after running 'docker build', their image contains an old version of a dependency even though they updated requirements.txt. They rebuild but Docker seems to skip re-installing dependencies. Why is this happening and how would you fix it?
questions.answer: Docker is reusing a cached layer. If requirements.txt is COPYed after other files or the install step's inputs didn't change hash, the RUN pip install layer is served from cache. Fix by COPYing requirements.txt before the app code and running install on it, so changes to it bust the cache. To force a clean build use --no-cache. Proper layer ordering keeps caching correct.

questions.question: Your app works on your laptop in Docker but fails in the pipeline. What differs?
questions.answer: Architecture, for example Apple M1 arm64 vs amd64 build agents, environment variables, build context and .dockerignore, cached layers, base image versions that moved, and network access during build. I pin base image versions and build with buildx for the right platform.

questions.question: Docker container cannot resolve DNS names but the host can. Debug?
questions.answer: I check /etc/resolv.conf inside the container, custom daemon DNS config, corporate VPN or firewall blocking UDP 53, and try --dns 8.8.8.8 to confirm. On user-defined networks I check the embedded DNS 127.0.0.11.

questions.question: A container keeps restarting under restart: always and hides the real error. How do you find it?
questions.answer: docker logs --tail and docker inspect for the exit code and restart count. I temporarily run it without the restart policy or override the entrypoint with sh to debug.

questions.question: A secret ended up in an image layer. Is deleting it in a later layer enough?
questions.answer: No. Earlier layers still contain it and anyone with the image can extract it. I rotate the secret, rebuild from clean, and use build secrets with BuildKit or runtime injection.

topics.name: CI/CD
topics.blurb: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, caching, deployment strategies, pipeline failures.

followUps.question: Pipeline takes 25 minutes. Where do you start optimising?
followUps.answer: Measure per-stage time first. Then dependency and Docker layer caching, run independent jobs in parallel, path filters so only affected parts run, and faster or larger runners where it pays off.

followUps.question: How do you handle secrets in pipelines?
followUps.answer: Store in the CI secret store or an external vault, inject at runtime as masked variables, and prefer OIDC federation to cloud roles instead of long-lived keys. Never print them or commit them, and scan repos for leaks.

followUps.question: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling?
followUps.answer: Rolling replaces instances gradually and is the simplest. Blue-green gives instant switch and rollback but needs double capacity. Canary exposes a small percentage first and is best for risky changes with good metrics.

followUps.question: A test fails randomly. What do you do?
followUps.answer: I rerun to confirm flakiness, look for shared state, timing, external dependencies, and test order issues. I quarantine it with a ticket rather than ignoring it, and fix the root cause so developers keep trusting the pipeline.

followUps.question: git revert vs git reset?
followUps.answer: Revert creates a new commit that undoes a change, safe on shared branches. Reset moves the branch pointer and rewrites history, so only for local or unpushed work.

followUps.question: Jenkins agent offline or builds stuck in queue. Steps?
followUps.answer: Check the agent connection and logs, disk space and Java process, executor count, and labels in the Jenkinsfile that must match the agent. For stability I use ephemeral agents in Kubernetes or Docker.

followUps.question: How do you stop bad code reaching production?
followUps.answer: Branch protection with required reviews, automated tests and security scans as required checks, environment approvals for prod, and automated rollback on failed health checks.

questions.question: Your team pushes code multiple times a day, but the CI pipeline takes 25 minutes because every run reinstalls dependencies and rebuilds the Docker image from scratch. Developers are frustrated by slow feedback. How would you speed up the pipeline?
questions.answer: Introduce caching: cache dependency directories (npm/pip/maven) keyed on lockfile hash, and use Docker layer caching (BuildKit, cache-from) so unchanged layers aren't rebuilt. Order Dockerfile so dependencies install before copying source. Split pipeline into parallel stages (lint/test/build). Use a persistent or warmer build agent, and only run full builds on relevant path changes.

questions.question: You're setting up a CI pipeline for a small team. A junior developer's merge request passes tests locally but fails in CI with 'command not found' errors. The code hasn't changed. What could be causing the difference and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: The CI environment differs from local — missing tools, different PATH, or dependencies not installed. Check the CI runner image and pipeline steps to ensure all required packages/tools are installed. Pin tool versions and use a consistent base image (Docker) matching local. Add explicit install steps and print versions for debugging. Standardizing environments prevents 'works on my machine' issues.

questions.question: A developer's feature branch build in your CI pipeline suddenly fails at the test stage with intermittent, different failures each run, while the same tests pass locally every time. What likely causes these flaky failures and how do you approach fixing them?
questions.answer: Flaky tests usually stem from shared state, race conditions, timing/async waits, test ordering, or external dependencies (network, DB). Reproduce by running tests repeatedly and in random order. Isolate the flaky test, add proper waits/mocks, avoid shared global state, and ensure clean fixtures per run. Quarantine the flaky test to unblock the team while fixing the root cause.

questions.question: You joined a team using GitHub Actions. A workflow that builds and pushes a Docker image to ECR fails at the push step with an authentication error, though the build succeeds. The AWS credentials are stored as repo secrets. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: Check that the AWS secrets are actually available to the job (secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered from forks/PRs). Verify the configure-aws-credentials step ran and the IAM user/role has ecr:GetAuthorizationToken and push permissions. Confirm you ran 'aws ecr get-login-password | docker login' before pushing, and that the ECR repo exists in the correct region/account. Check token expiry and correct registry URL.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys to staging automatically, but the team wants production deploys to require a manual approval step after staging passes. How would you design this in your pipeline?
questions.answer: Split the pipeline into stages: build/test, deploy-staging (automatic), then deploy-production gated by a manual approval. Use the tool's approval/gate feature (e.g. GitHub Actions environments with required reviewers, GitLab manual jobs, or Jenkins input step). Restrict who can approve, keep the same artifact promoted through stages, and log who approved for auditability.

questions.question: You're setting up your first CI pipeline for a Python project. The build passes but you realize secrets like the database password are being printed in the pipeline logs when tests run. How do you fix this and prevent leaks?
questions.answer: Store secrets in the CI's secret store (masked variables/repo secrets), not in code or plain env files. Ensure the CI masks them in logs. Remove any echo/print of env vars and disable debug logging that dumps environment. Rotate the exposed password immediately. Use least-privilege credentials scoped to the pipeline only.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline builds a Docker image and tags every build as 'latest', pushing to your registry. A rollback is needed after a bad deploy, but you realize 'latest' was overwritten and you can't identify or pull the previous good image. How would you fix your tagging strategy?
questions.answer: Stop relying on 'latest' for deploys. Tag images with immutable identifiers like the Git commit SHA or a semantic version (e.g. app:1.4.2 or app:sha-abc123). Keep 'latest' as a convenience pointer only. This lets you pin deployments and roll back to any specific previous tag. Enable registry image retention/immutability policies.

questions.question: A teammate deleted a file from a Git repo and committed, but the file contained a large binary that's still bloating the repo. Cloning is now painfully slow for everyone. As the junior on the team, how would you reduce the repo size safely?
questions.answer: Simply deleting a file only removes it from the latest commit; it stays in history. Use git filter-repo (or BFG Repo-Cleaner) to purge the blob from all commits, then force-push. Coordinate with the team since history rewriting breaks existing clones. Going forward, add large binaries to Git LFS and update .gitignore.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline runs unit tests then integration tests that need a database. The integration stage fails randomly because the DB container isn't ready when tests start, even though it was started in a prior step. How do you fix this?
questions.answer: The DB process being 'started' doesn't mean it's accepting connections. Add a readiness wait: poll the port/health with a retry loop (e.g., wait-for-it, pg_isready, or a healthcheck) before running tests. Use service containers with healthchecks so CI waits for 'healthy'. Avoid fixed sleeps; wait on actual readiness to eliminate the race.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline builds and deploys on every push to main, but a bad commit went straight to production because nothing validated the build artifact. The team wants a safety gate that still keeps deploys fast. How would you design the pipeline?
questions.answer: Add stages: build → automated tests/linting → build immutable artifact → deploy to staging → smoke/health checks → deploy to prod. Only promote the same tested artifact forward. Use fail-fast on tests and optionally a canary or automated rollback on health-check failure. Keep prod deploy gated on passing checks so speed is retained but bad builds are blocked.

questions.question: Your team uses GitHub Actions to deploy to multiple environments. The workflow duplicates the same 40 lines of build steps across dev, staging, and prod jobs, and a recent bug fix had to be copy-pasted three times, causing one env to be missed. How would you restructure this?
questions.answer: Extract shared logic into a reusable workflow (workflow_call) or a composite action, then call it per environment with inputs/matrix. Use environment-specific variables/secrets via GitHub Environments. This DRYs the pipeline so fixes apply everywhere at once and reduces drift between environments.

questions.question: Your team deploys with a blue-green strategy on AWS using two target groups behind an ALB. After switching traffic to green, users report errors, and you need to roll back fast. What's the quickest safe rollback and what should you verify afterward?
questions.answer: Switch the ALB listener rule back to the blue target group to instantly restore the known-good version, since blue is still running. Verify health checks pass on blue, confirm error rates drop in monitoring, and drain green connections. Then investigate green's failures in a non-prod path before retrying. Blue-green's key benefit is this instant rollback with no redeploy.

questions.question: A teammate created a Jenkins pipeline that clones a large monorepo on every run, and builds now take 20+ minutes just fetching Git history. Actual compile time is under 3 minutes. As a junior, how would you speed up the checkout?
questions.answer: Use a shallow clone (--depth 1) and single-branch fetch so you don't pull full history. Enable Git reference/mirror caching or persistent workspace caching on the agent. For monorepos, use sparse-checkout to fetch only needed paths. This cuts network and disk I/O dramatically without changing build logic.

questions.question: Your GitHub Actions CI builds fine, but deploys to AWS started failing after a teammate rotated the IAM access keys stored as secrets. You want to stop storing long-lived keys entirely. How would you redesign authentication?
questions.answer: Replace static keys with OIDC: configure GitHub as an OIDC identity provider in AWS IAM, create a role with a trust policy scoped to your repo/branch, and use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume. This gives short-lived, auto-rotated credentials, removes secrets from the repo, and lets you tightly scope permissions per workflow.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline runs a suite of tests that pass locally and on most runs, but roughly one in five pipeline runs fails on a different test each time with no code change. Developers are re-running until green. How would you investigate and stabilize these flaky tests?
questions.answer: Identify flaky tests by tracking which fail intermittently across runs. Common causes: shared state between tests, timing/race conditions, reliance on external services, or test ordering. Isolate by running tests in random order and in parallel. Fix by adding proper waits/retries for async ops, mocking external calls, and cleaning state between tests. Quarantine flaky tests so they don't block deploys while being fixed.

questions.question: You're setting up a new GitHub Actions CI job for a Node app. Every run reinstalls all npm dependencies from scratch, adding several minutes. A senior asks you to cut build time. What's your approach?
questions.answer: Add dependency caching using actions/cache keyed on the OS and a hash of package-lock.json, caching ~/.npm or node_modules. Use 'npm ci' for reproducible installs. On cache hit installs are near-instant; on lockfile change the key changes and it refreshes. Also consider setup-node's built-in cache option which handles this automatically.

questions.question: A developer's CI job needs to run on every pull request to run tests, but you notice it also triggers full deploys on draft/PR builds, occasionally pushing untested code. How would you restructure the pipeline triggers so tests run on PRs but deploys only happen on merges to main?
questions.answer: Separate concerns with trigger filters: run test jobs on pull_request events (any branch), and gate deploy jobs to only run on push to main (or after merge). In GitHub Actions use 'on: pull_request' for tests and 'on: push: branches: [main]' for deploy, or add conditional 'if: github.ref == refs/heads/main'. This ensures deploys only fire post-merge.

questions.question: You're a junior engineer asked to give a new teammate the ability to run a build job in Jenkins but not configure or delete other jobs. Currently everyone shares an admin login. How would you set this up properly?
questions.answer: Enable Jenkins security with individual accounts (or SSO/LDAP) instead of a shared admin. Use Matrix-based or Role-based Authorization Strategy to grant the teammate only Job/Build and Job/Read on the relevant jobs, not Administer or Configure/Delete. Verify by logging in as them. This follows least-privilege and gives an audit trail per user.

questions.question: Your team wants merges to the main branch to automatically deploy, but only after a senior manually approves the production step. Right now the pipeline deploys straight through with no gate. How would you add a manual approval before prod using your CI/CD tool?
questions.answer: Split the pipeline into build/test, deploy-to-staging, and deploy-to-prod stages. Put a manual approval gate before the prod stage—in GitHub Actions use an Environment with required reviewers, in GitLab a 'when: manual' job, in Jenkins an 'input' step. The pipeline pauses until an authorized reviewer approves, so automated tests still run fast but production requires human sign-off.

questions.question: Your GitHub Actions workflow needs to deploy to AWS, but it currently runs sequential jobs that each spin up and repeat setup steps, making the pipeline slow. You want build artifacts produced once and reused by later deploy jobs. How would you structure this?
questions.answer: Split into a build job that produces artifacts and deploy jobs that depend on it via 'needs'. Use actions/upload-artifact in build and actions/download-artifact in deploy jobs so you build once. Use caching for dependencies. Parallelize independent jobs and gate deploy on build success. This avoids redundant work and speeds the pipeline.

questions.question: After promoting a new build through your CI/CD pipeline, staging works but production fails because an environment-specific config value is wrong. Configs are currently copy-pasted per environment in the pipeline. How would you restructure this to prevent such mismatches?
questions.answer: Externalize config from the pipeline: keep a single build artifact and inject env-specific values at deploy time (env vars, config maps, or a secrets/parameter store like SSM/Vault). Use per-environment value files validated in CI. Add a promotion step that reuses the exact same artifact across envs so only config differs. Validate configs with schema checks before deploy to catch bad values early.

questions.question: Your team wants every push to a feature branch to run linting and unit tests automatically, but a teammate's commits keep skipping the pipeline entirely. The workflow file exists in main but not always in feature branches. Why might CI not trigger and how do you ensure it runs on all branches?
questions.answer: GitHub Actions runs the workflow file present in the branch being pushed, so if the feature branch was created before the workflow existed (or was deleted there), CI won't run. Ensure the workflow file is merged/present in the branch, set proper 'on: push' branch filters (or '**'), and rebase/merge main so all branches include the workflow.

questions.question: Your team's GitHub Actions workflow needs to deploy only when code is pushed to main, but right now it runs on every push to every branch, wasting runners and sometimes deploying feature code. How would you restrict deployment to main only?
questions.answer: Scope the trigger with branch filters: on: push: branches: [main]. For a shared workflow, gate the deploy job with a condition like if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'. Keep lint/test steps running on all branches but restrict the deploy job. Optionally use environments with required reviewers for extra protection on production deploys.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys a new app version, but you want to release it to only 10% of production traffic first and gradually increase if error rates stay low. Currently deploys switch 100% of traffic at once. How would you implement this?
questions.answer: Implement a canary deployment. Route a small percentage of traffic to the new version using a service mesh (Istio), an ingress with weighted routing, or two target groups behind an ALB with weighted listener rules. Monitor error rate/latency metrics for the canary; if healthy, gradually shift weights up, otherwise roll back. Tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger can automate this with metric-based analysis.

questions.question: Your production deploy uses a blue-green strategy on AWS. After switching the ALB to the green environment, users report intermittent errors and stale sessions, even though green passed health checks. Rolling back to blue fixes it. How would you diagnose and prevent this class of issue?
questions.answer: Intermittent errors after cutover often stem from in-flight requests, sticky sessions tied to blue, or shared state (cache/DB) mismatched with green's schema. Diagnose via ALB access logs, target group metrics, and app logs correlating errors to the cutover time. Prevent by draining connections (deregistration delay), disabling/warming sticky sessions, ensuring backward-compatible schema/session store (shared Redis), and doing a canary before …

questions.question: Your GitHub Actions CI pipeline passes locally-run tests but intermittently fails in CI with flaky test errors and different results between runs. The tests hit a real shared database that multiple pipeline runs use simultaneously. How would you make the pipeline reliable?
questions.answer: The shared DB causes race conditions between concurrent runs. Isolate each run's state: spin up an ephemeral DB per job using a service container (e.g. Postgres service in the workflow), or use isolated schemas/namespaces per run. Ensure tests set up and tear down their own fixtures and don't rely on shared mutable data. This makes runs deterministic and parallel-safe.

questions.question: Your GitHub Actions workflow fails at the build step with 'permission denied' when running a script, but only in CI — it works on your machine. The repo was cloned fresh by the runner. How would you fix this?
questions.answer: The script likely lost its executable bit in Git. Check with git ls-files --stage script.sh; if the mode is 100644 it's not executable. Fix by running git update-index --chmod=+x script.sh and committing, or invoke it with bash script.sh in the workflow. This ensures the executable permission is tracked in the repo for all runners.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline needs to deploy to a Kubernetes cluster, but the deploy job intermittently fails with 'unable to connect to the server: dial tcp: i/o timeout' while other jobs succeed. The kubeconfig and credentials are correct. How would you diagnose this?
questions.answer: Intermittent timeouts suggest network reachability rather than auth. Check if the cluster API endpoint is private and the runner is outside the allowed CIDR/VPC, or hitting an IP allowlist. Verify DNS resolution of the API server, any load balancer health, and whether self-hosted runners lose network. Fix by ensuring runners have stable, whitelisted access (VPC peering, authorized networks) and add retries for transient blips.

questions.question: Your team's CI/CD pipeline runs unit tests, builds a Docker image, and deploys — all in one long sequential job that takes 40 minutes. Developers wait a long time for feedback even on small changes. How would you restructure the pipeline to give faster feedback and reduce wasted work?
questions.answer: Split into stages/parallel jobs: run lint and unit tests first and in parallel so failures surface fast, then build only if tests pass, then deploy. Cache dependencies and Docker layers between runs. Run fast checks on every push and heavier integration/deploy steps only on main. Use fail-fast and only rebuild what changed to cut feedback time.

questions.question: Your team wants zero-downtime database schema migrations in your CI/CD pipeline, but currently deploys briefly break because new app code expects a column that the migration adds at the same time. How would you restructure the process?
questions.answer: Use the expand-and-contract pattern. First deploy a backward-compatible migration (add nullable column) that old and new code both tolerate. Then deploy app code that writes/reads the new column. Once all instances run new code, run a contract migration to remove old columns/backfill. Decouple migration steps from app deploy in the pipeline so schema changes are always compatible with both versions running simultaneously.

questions.question: Your GitLab CI pipeline deploys to production on every merge to main, but the team now wants a manual approval gate before prod and automatic deploys to staging. They also want the same build artifact promoted, not rebuilt for prod. How would you restructure the pipeline?
questions.answer: Build the artifact/image once in an early stage and store it (registry with an immutable tag or SHA). Auto-deploy that same artifact to staging. Add a separate prod deploy job set to when: manual (or a protected environment with required approvers) that only promotes the already-built image—no rebuild. Use environment protection and only allow authorized users to trigger the prod job, ensuring build-once-deploy-many consistency.

questions.question: Your team stores application secrets (DB passwords, API keys) as plaintext environment variables in the GitHub Actions workflow YAML. Security flagged this. You need to inject secrets into deploys securely without exposing them in logs or the repo. How would you redesign this?
questions.answer: Move secrets out of YAML into GitHub Actions encrypted secrets (or an external vault like AWS Secrets Manager/HashiCorp Vault) referenced via ${{ secrets.NAME }}. GitHub masks these in logs. For AWS, use OIDC to assume a role and pull secrets at runtime instead of storing long-lived keys. Rotate the already-exposed secrets, restrict secret access by environment, and avoid echoing them in scripts.

questions.question: Your team's Jenkins pipeline has started failing on the 'checkout' stage with an error about the Git credentials being invalid, but the same repo clones fine from your laptop using your personal token. The pipeline hasn't changed in weeks. How would you diagnose and fix this?
questions.answer: Check if the Jenkins credential (PAT/deploy key) expired or was rotated — most managed tokens have expiry. Look at the exact Git error in console output. Verify the credential ID referenced in the pipeline still exists and maps to a valid secret. Generate a new token/deploy key with correct repo scope, update the Jenkins credential, and re-run. Prefer machine/deploy keys or a bot account with long-lived, scoped access over personal tokens.

questions.question: A developer reports that after a git push, the CI job clones the repo but fails at a build step with 'permission denied' when running a shell script (./build.sh). The script exists in the repo and runs fine on their laptop. How would you diagnose and fix this?
questions.answer: The script likely lost its executable bit. Check git ls-files -s build.sh; mode 100644 means not executable. Fix by chmod +x build.sh && git update-index --chmod=+x build.sh then commit, or invoke it as bash build.sh in the pipeline. Ensure core.filemode isn't hiding the change. Verify on a fresh clone.

questions.question: Your GitHub Actions CI reruns identical dependency installation and builds on every push, making pipelines slow and expensive. The same dependencies rarely change. How would you speed up the pipeline?
questions.answer: Add dependency caching with actions/cache (or setup-* built-in caching), keyed on a lockfile hash (e.g. package-lock.json) so cache invalidates only when deps change. Use Docker layer caching (buildx + registry/gha cache) for image builds. Split into parallel jobs and only run affected stages via path filters. Cache build outputs where safe. Result: cache hits skip reinstalls, cutting runtime significantly.

questions.question: After merging a change, your GitHub Actions workflow that deploys to production ran automatically on a feature branch push and nearly deployed untested code. You need to ensure prod deploys only happen on main merges and require approval. How would you restructure this?
questions.answer: Scope the deploy trigger to on: push: branches: [main] or to release tags, not all branches. Split build/test from deploy into separate jobs with needs. Use a GitHub Environment named 'production' with required reviewers for a manual approval gate. Restrict who can approve. Separate staging (auto) from prod (gated) jobs.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline builds and tests fine, but deployments to production occasionally succeed in the pipeline while the app is actually broken for users. There's no verification after deploy. How would you add confidence that a deploy is truly healthy before declaring success?
questions.answer: Add post-deploy smoke tests and health checks against the live environment (hit key endpoints, check readiness). Use a progressive rollout (canary/rolling) with automated metric checks on error rate and latency, and auto-rollback on failure. Gate the pipeline's 'success' on these verifications rather than just the deploy command exit code.

questions.question: A teammate asks you to roll back a merged change in your Git repo that introduced a bug in production, but other important commits were made after it on main. You must not lose the newer work. How would you safely undo just the bad change?
questions.answer: Use git revert <bad-commit-sha> which creates a new commit that undoes those changes while preserving history and later commits. For a merge commit, use git revert -m 1 <sha>. Avoid git reset --hard on a shared branch since it rewrites history and loses later work. Push the revert, verify in a pipeline, then deploy.

questions.question: You are a mid-level engineer. Your CI/CD pipeline uses a 'docker build' step that is consistently failing on an 'npm install' step only in the CI environment, but not on developer machines. How do you troubleshoot this difference?
questions.answer: Check the CI runner's resource limits; it may be hitting memory caps. Verify the 'npm' cache settings and ensure the CI environment has appropriate egress access to the registry (as it may be restricted vs local machines). Inspect the Dockerfile for hidden dependencies like 'git' or build-essential packages that exist on dev laptops but are missing from the CI runner's base image.

questions.question: A GitHub Actions runner is failing because it cannot pull a private Docker image. How do you debug the authentication flow without exposing credentials?
questions.answer: First, verify the secret scope in the repository settings. Then, add a temporary 'docker login' step in the pipeline using 'echo $SECRET | docker login ... --password-stdin' to test authentication. Check the runner logs to confirm if the error is an 'access denied' (permissions) or 'connection timeout' (network).

questions.question: After merging a change, your CI/CD pipeline built and pushed a Docker image tagged 'latest', but the Kubernetes cluster didn't pull the new image on rollout—pods still run old code despite a successful deploy. Why, and how would you fix this reliably?
questions.answer: With the mutable 'latest' tag and imagePullPolicy behavior, Kubernetes may reuse the cached image since the tag string is unchanged. Best fix: use immutable, unique tags per build (e.g., git SHA) so each deploy references a new image, forcing a pull and clean rollout. As a stopgap, set imagePullPolicy: Always, but unique tags also improve rollback and traceability.

questions.question: Your team wants zero-downtime database schema migrations during CI/CD deploys. Currently the migration runs as part of app startup, and during a rolling update old and new pods run simultaneously against the same DB, causing errors when the new schema breaks old code. How would you structure migrations to avoid this?
questions.answer: Use backward-compatible, expand/contract migrations. Phase 1: additive changes (new columns/tables) that old code ignores. Deploy new code that uses both. Phase 2: after all pods run new code, run contract migration to remove old columns. Run migrations as a separate step/Job, not on app startup, so ordering is controlled and both app versions stay compatible during rollout.

questions.question: Your team wants CI builds to run faster. The pipeline reinstalls all npm dependencies from scratch on every run, adding 4-5 minutes each time, even when package.json hasn't changed. How would you speed this up in your CI/CD tool?
questions.answer: Add dependency caching keyed on the lockfile hash (e.g. package-lock.json). In GitHub Actions use actions/cache or setup-node's built-in cache with a key like hash of the lockfile. On cache hit, deps restore instantly; on miss, they reinstall and repopulate the cache. This avoids redundant downloads while auto-invalidating when dependencies actually change.

questions.question: Your team's Jenkins pipeline deploys artifacts to a server over SSH, but the deploy stage fails with 'Host key verification failed' whenever it runs on a freshly provisioned build agent, though it works on the old agent. How would you diagnose and fix this so deploys work on any agent?
questions.answer: The new agent has no entry for the target host in its known_hosts, so SSH refuses. Fix by adding the host key ahead of time: run ssh-keyscan target-host >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts in a setup step, or use a managed known_hosts credential. Avoid disabling StrictHostKeyChecking blindly in prod as it opens MITM risk; prefer pre-seeding verified keys.

questions.question: A developer complains that after they push code, the GitHub Actions workflow runs but always uses a stale version of a helper script stored in the repo. They just committed a fix to that script, yet the pipeline still runs the old logic. The workflow uses actions/checkout. What would you check to ensure the pipeline runs the latest committed code?
questions.answer: Confirm the workflow triggered on the correct commit (check the run's commit SHA vs their push). Ensure actions/checkout isn't pinned to a ref/branch or using a cached path, and that fetch-depth is adequate. Check for caching steps restoring old files, and that the script isn't being overwritten by a cache or artifact. Verify they pushed to the branch the workflow listens on.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline builds a Docker image, runs tests inside it, and pushes to ECR, but the push step intermittently fails with 'no basic auth credentials'. The AWS credentials in the pipeline are valid and other AWS calls succeed. What causes this and how do you fix it reliably?
questions.answer: Having valid AWS credentials isn't enough—Docker needs an ECR login token, which expires after 12 hours. Intermittent failures usually mean a stale/missing docker login. Fix by authenticating right before push: aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <acct>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com. Ensure the IAM role has ECR push permissions and login runs in the same job as the push.

questions.question: A deployment to prod succeeded in the pipeline but users see the old version. Why?
questions.answer: Cache layers like CDN or browser cache, image tag not changed so Kubernetes did not roll out, a rollout still in progress, or the deploy went to a different environment or cluster. I verify the running image digest.

questions.question: Someone force-pushed to main and wiped commits. How do you recover?
questions.answer: Use git reflog on any clone that had the commits, or the CI runner and GitHub PR refs, then push the restored commit. Then enable branch protection to forbid force pushes.

questions.question: The same pipeline passes on one branch and fails on another with identical code. Why?
questions.answer: Different variables or secrets scoped per branch or environment, cache poisoning, a different base commit, or conditional logic in the pipeline. I diff the environment and clear the cache.

questions.question: Your pipeline deploys to prod on every merge and a bad release goes out Friday evening. How do you improve the process?
questions.answer: Add automated smoke tests and canary with auto-rollback, deployment windows or approvals for risky changes, feature flags, and clear rollback runbooks so recovery takes minutes.

topics.name: Terraform
topics.blurb: State, modules, environments, drift, imports, safe applies.

followUps.question: Why remote state and what is state locking?
followUps.answer: Remote state gives the team one source of truth and encryption. Locking, for example with DynamoDB or S3 native locking, prevents two applies from corrupting the state at the same time.

followUps.question: How do you stop Terraform from destroying a critical resource?
followUps.answer: prevent_destroy in lifecycle, careful plan review in CI, and restricted prod apply permissions. For a rename I use moved blocks or terraform state mv so it is not recreated.

followUps.question: Someone changed a resource manually in the console. How do you handle drift?
followUps.answer: terraform plan shows the drift. I decide whether to revert it with apply or update the code to match. I also restrict console write access and run scheduled drift detection.

followUps.question: Workspaces or separate directories for environments?
followUps.answer: Workspaces share code and are good for small cases, but are easy to confuse. For prod I prefer separate directories or backends per environment with shared modules and tfvars, so a wrong apply cannot touch another environment.

followUps.question: How do you bring existing infrastructure under Terraform?
followUps.answer: Write the resource block, run terraform import or an import block, then run plan until it shows no changes. I do this one resource at a time to avoid surprises.

followUps.question: Secrets in Terraform state: risk and fix?
followUps.answer: State can contain secrets in plain text, so the backend must be encrypted with tight access. I mark variables sensitive, pull secrets from Secrets Manager or Vault, and avoid hardcoding them in code.

followUps.question: count vs for_each?
followUps.answer: count uses index, so removing a middle item shifts and recreates later resources. for_each uses stable keys, so it is safer for collections that change.

followUps.question: Apply failed with state lock error. What do you do?
followUps.answer: First check nobody is running an apply, the pipeline included. If the lock is stale, I use terraform force-unlock with the lock ID. Never unlock while a run is active.

questions.question: A colleague pushed a change to a shared Terraform state, and now your local 'terraform plan' shows drift and unexpected changes to resources you didn't touch. The team uses a single state file with no locking. How do you handle this safely?
questions.answer: First run 'terraform plan' to understand the drift without applying. Coordinate with the team to freeze changes. Enable remote state with locking (S3 + DynamoDB) to prevent concurrent writes. Use 'terraform refresh'/'terraform state' commands to reconcile. Review who changed what via version control and state history. Only apply after confirming intended changes to avoid clobbering a teammate's work.

questions.question: You manage a Terraform module for provisioning VPCs. A teammate ran 'terraform apply' and now the plan wants to change subnet CIDRs that no one edited. You suspect someone modified resources manually in the AWS console. How do you reconcile the actual infrastructure with your Terraform code without downtime?
questions.answer: Run 'terraform plan' to see the drift, then use 'terraform refresh'/plan to understand current state. For manual changes you want to keep, update the .tf code to match reality. Use 'terraform import' if resources exist outside state. Avoid blind apply—review each change, especially destructive ones. Communicate to enforce no manual changes going forward and consider drift detection.

questions.question: Your company uses Terraform to manage AWS. A new engineer wants to test changes but is worried about accidentally affecting production infrastructure since everyone shares the same AWS account and state. How would you structure Terraform to safely separate environments?
questions.answer: Use separate state files per environment via workspaces or, better, separate backend configs/directories (dev, staging, prod). Store state remotely in S3 with DynamoDB locking. Parameterize with tfvars per environment. Consider separate AWS accounts for real isolation. Enforce plan review and least-privilege IAM. This prevents a dev apply from touching prod resources.

questions.question: Your Terraform config provisions an S3 bucket and an IAM policy referencing it. On a fresh apply it fails with a dependency error because the policy is created before the bucket exists, but sometimes it works. How do you make the ordering reliable?
questions.answer: The intermittent behavior comes from Terraform's parallel resource creation without an explicit dependency. Reference the bucket's attribute (e.g., aws_s3_bucket.this.arn) directly in the policy so Terraform infers the dependency graph, or add an explicit 'depends_on'. Attribute references are preferred as they build a correct DAG automatically.

questions.question: You manage Terraform for infra. After importing an existing manually-created load balancer into state, terraform plan still wants to make many changes to it even though nothing should change. How do you reconcile this?
questions.answer: Import only brings the resource into state, not its full configuration. The plan diff means your HCL doesn't match reality. Run 'terraform plan' to see each attribute drift, then update your resource block to match the actual settings (from console/CLI describe) until plan shows no changes. Iterate attribute by attribute. Consider 'terraform plan -refresh-only' to inspect current state.

questions.question: You're deploying infrastructure with Terraform across a team, but two engineers ran apply at the same time and corrupted the state file, causing conflicting resources. How would you prevent this from happening again?
questions.answer: Move state to a remote backend like S3 with DynamoDB state locking (or Terraform Cloud). Locking prevents concurrent applies. Enable versioning on the S3 bucket so you can recover prior state. Standardize on the remote backend for all team members and never keep state local for shared infra.

questions.question: You maintain a Terraform config that provisions EC2 instances. A colleague adds a new instance and runs 'terraform apply', but it fails saying the resource already exists in AWS. The instance was actually created manually last week to match a spec. How do you bring it under Terraform management without recreating it?
questions.answer: Use 'terraform import aws_instance.name i-xxxx' to map the existing instance into state. Then run 'terraform plan' and adjust the HCL config until the plan shows no changes, so Terraform's code matches reality. Never delete/recreate. Commit the config and communicate to the team so no more manual instances are made.

questions.question: Your team manages AWS with Terraform. A new security requirement says all EC2 instances must have a specific tag. Rather than checking manually after each apply, you want to enforce this so non-compliant configs fail before deploy. How would you implement this?
questions.answer: Add a policy-as-code check in the pipeline: run 'terraform plan -out' then evaluate with a tool like OPA/Conftest or tfsec/Checkov against the plan JSON to reject resources missing the tag. Optionally use Terraform default_tags at the provider level to auto-apply org tags, and add validation. Fail the pipeline on violations before apply.

questions.question: Your team runs a Terraform-managed VPC and needs to add a new private subnet for a database tier. A colleague worries that applying could disrupt existing running instances. How do you safely add the subnet and confirm no existing resources are affected?
questions.answer: Add the new subnet resource, then run 'terraform plan' and carefully review the output—it should show only the new subnet being created (+ add) with no changes/destroys to existing resources. If plan shows unexpected modifications, investigate before applying. Use targeted apply if needed. Version control the change and get it peer-reviewed via PR.

questions.question: Your team runs a Terraform-managed set of resources, and after a colleague manually changed a security group rule in the AWS console, the next terraform plan shows it wants to revert the change. The colleague insists their change is needed. How do you resolve this drift correctly?
questions.answer: This is configuration drift. Don't just apply and overwrite. Decide the source of truth: if the manual change is valid, update the Terraform code (the security_group_rule) to match so plan is clean; then apply. If it was unauthorized, apply to restore desired state. Going forward, restrict console write access and use terraform plan in CI to detect drift early.

questions.question: You maintain a Terraform module used by several teams. After you released a new module version, one team's terraform apply unexpectedly wants to destroy and recreate their database because you renamed a resource block internally. They're panicking about data loss. How do you avoid the destroy and safely ship the rename?
questions.answer: Renaming a resource block changes its address, so Terraform sees the old one as removed and plans a destroy/create. Prevent this with moved {} blocks in the module (or terraform state mv) to map the old address to the new one so Terraform treats it as a rename, not a replacement. Also add prevent_destroy on stateful resources as a safety net and communicate the upgrade path clearly.

questions.question: Your team provisions an EC2 instance with Terraform and uses a user_data script to install and configure the app on boot. A teammate updated the user_data script and ran apply, expecting the change to take effect, but the running instance still uses the old setup. Why, and how do you apply it?
questions.answer: user_data only runs at first boot; changing it doesn't re-run on existing instances. By default Terraform may not even replace the instance unless user_data_replace_on_change is set. To apply, either set user_data_replace_on_change=true (or taint the instance) so Terraform recreates it, or SSH in and run the new steps manually. Recreation may cause downtime, so plan accordingly.

questions.question: After applying a Terraform change to add a new tag to all EC2 instances, the plan shows it also wants to modify unrelated attributes like AMI and instance_type that no one changed. You're worried apply will replace instances. How do you investigate and apply only the tag safely?
questions.answer: Read the plan carefully to see if changes are in-place (~) or replacements (-/+). AMI/type drift often means the config drifted from real state or a data source resolved a new AMI. Run 'terraform plan' with -refresh, pin the AMI to a fixed ID or use lifecycle ignore_changes for AMI, and use -target on the tag change if urgent. Reconcile the config so plan is clean before broad apply.

questions.question: A Terraform apply failed halfway through creating a set of resources, leaving state that partially matches reality. Now every plan errors out or shows confusing diffs, and a teammate wants to just delete the state file and start over. Why is that dangerous, and how do you recover cleanly?
questions.answer: Deleting state orphans real resources — Terraform loses track and may try to recreate duplicates. Instead: run terraform plan to see the delta, use terraform state list to inspect what's tracked. Import any real-but-untracked resources with terraform import. Remove stale entries with terraform state rm if the resource was destroyed. Then re-run apply to converge. Always back up the state file first.

questions.question: Your CI pipeline runs Terraform for multiple teams, but two pipelines occasionally apply at the same time and corrupt each other's changes because they share one state file with no locking. How would you make concurrent runs safe and isolate teams?
questions.answer: Use a remote backend that supports state locking, e.g. S3 backend with a DynamoDB lock table. Locking blocks concurrent applies so runs queue safely. Isolate teams/environments with separate state files via distinct backend keys or Terraform workspaces, so each pipeline manages its own state. Add plan-then-apply gating in CI to reduce conflicts.

questions.question: After applying Terraform for a new EC2 instance, the apply succeeds but you realize you need to change the instance type. When you update the type and run apply, Terraform wants to destroy and recreate the instance, which would lose the data. How would you handle this?
questions.answer: Changing instance type is normally an in-place update, but destroy/recreate suggests a forces-new-resource attribute changed (like AMI). Run terraform plan and read the '# forces replacement' notes to see what triggers it. If only type changed, it updates in place after a stop/start. To protect data, ensure the root volume isn't deleted on termination, or move data to a separate EBS volume/EFS. Use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on c…

questions.question: A developer reports that after running terraform apply, their change didn't take effect because someone else's changes overwrote the state. They both keep local terraform.tfstate files on their laptops and share it via Slack. Why is this fragile, and how would you fix state management for a team?
questions.answer: Local state on laptops has no locking, no single source of truth, and gets out of sync — leading to overwrites and drift. Move state to a shared remote backend like S3 with DynamoDB for locking (or Terraform Cloud). This gives one authoritative state, prevents concurrent applies, and enables versioning/rollback. Remove local tfstate from Git and never share it manually.

questions.question: You're a mid-level engineer managing infrastructure with Terraform. A teammate accidentally deleted an S3 bucket resource block, and the next apply plans to destroy the live bucket that holds production data. You catch it in the plan before applying. How would you keep the resource but stop Terraform from destroying it?
questions.answer: Don't apply the destructive plan. To protect it, add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on the resource so Terraform errors instead of deleting. If the block was removed, restore it (from Git) so state and config match. Alternatively terraform state rm to stop managing it. Also enable S3 versioning and consider deletion protection for critical data.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys a Terraform change to an AWS environment, but the apply hangs for 20+ minutes on creating an RDS instance and eventually times out. Re-running sometimes succeeds. Other resources apply quickly. How would you diagnose and make this reliable?
questions.answer: RDS creation legitimately takes 10-20+ min, so a short pipeline/Terraform timeout is the likely culprit. Set an appropriate timeouts block on the resource and increase the CI job timeout. Check whether a dependency (subnet group, parameter group) or capacity/quota issue delays provisioning. Review CloudTrail/RDS events for the actual bottleneck rather than assuming Terraform is stuck.

questions.question: Your Terraform-managed AWS security group has drifted — someone added an inbound rule manually via the console during an incident. The next terraform plan wants to remove it, but the team wants to keep the change now that it's needed. How would you reconcile this safely?
questions.answer: Don't just apply and wipe it. Confirm the manual rule is legitimate, then codify it: add the corresponding ingress block to the Terraform config so plan shows no changes. Run terraform plan to verify zero diff, document the change, and consider drift detection (scheduled plans) and stricter console access to prevent unmanaged edits going forward.

questions.question: Your team's Terraform code provisions infra across dev, staging, and prod, but everyone edits the same directory and hardcodes values per environment, causing frequent mistakes when applying to the wrong environment. How would you restructure this for safe multi-environment management?
questions.answer: Separate state per environment using workspaces or, better, per-env directories/backends with distinct state files. Extract shared logic into reusable modules and pass env-specific values via tfvars files. Use separate backend configs (e.g. different S3 keys) so a wrong apply can't touch another env. Enforce plan review in CI and require explicit -var-file selection to prevent misapplies.

questions.question: Your Terraform module creates an IAM role and an EC2 instance that uses it, but terraform apply intermittently fails with 'iam instance profile not found' when creating the instance. Re-running fixes it. How would you make this reliable?
questions.answer: It's a race/eventual-consistency issue: IAM instance profile propagation lags behind creation. Ensure Terraform knows the dependency by referencing the profile's attribute in the instance (implicit depends), or add depends_on = [aws_iam_instance_profile.this]. For propagation delay, add a time_sleep resource or retry. Best practice: reference aws_iam_instance_profile.name directly so the dependency graph enforces correct ordering.

questions.question: After a Terraform apply, a critical EC2 instance was replaced (destroyed and recreated) even though you only intended to change a tag. This caused unexpected downtime. How would you investigate why it replaced instead of updated, and prevent it in future?
questions.answer: Run terraform plan and read the plan carefully — replacements show '-/+' and list the attribute forcing replacement (e.g. changing a subnet, AMI, or user_data). Some attributes are 'ForceNew'. To prevent surprise downtime, always review plans in CI, use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources, and create_before_destroy where recreation is unavoidable. Avoid touching force-new attributes casually.

questions.question: A teammate's Terraform apply fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock' and won't proceed. They say their previous apply was interrupted (laptop crashed). No one else is running Terraform. How would you resolve this safely?
questions.answer: The interrupted run left a stale lock in the backend (e.g. DynamoDB for S3 backend). First confirm nobody is actually applying. Read the lock ID/info from the error message, then run terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> to release it. Verify state integrity with terraform plan afterward. Avoid manually editing the lock table unless force-unlock fails. Going forward, ensure applies run in CI so interrupted local runs don't leave locks.

questions.question: Your team's Terraform state is stored in an S3 backend, but two engineers ran apply from different branches with different variable values, and now the deployed infra doesn't match anyone's code. Future plans show confusing diffs. How would you recover and prevent recurrence?
questions.answer: Run terraform plan to see drift, reconcile by picking the intended config and applying from a single source of truth (main branch). Enable state locking via DynamoDB to prevent concurrent applies. Enforce applies only through CI on merged main, not local runs. Use terraform state inspection and consider workspaces/separate state per env. Document a single apply path.

questions.question: Your Terraform code manages an S3 bucket that another team manually configured last month with lifecycle rules and bucket policies. You need to bring it under Terraform management without destroying and recreating it or losing its existing config. How would you approach this?
questions.answer: Write the resource block matching the existing bucket, then run terraform import aws_s3_bucket.name bucket-name to add it to state without recreating it. Run terraform plan and reconcile the diffs—add lifecycle rules, policy, versioning etc. to code until plan shows no changes. Use terraform state show to see imported attributes. Commit once plan is clean so Terraform matches reality.

questions.question: A mid-level engineer realizes that a Terraform-managed production database cluster is performing poorly. The team suspects a manual index was added via the console, but applying the current Terraform code would overwrite it. How do you safely synchronize?
questions.answer: Do not edit state files manually. First, use 'terraform plan' to see the drift. Identify the missing index/configuration and update the Terraform code to match the desired state of the database including that index. Run a plan again to ensure the desired configuration is now correctly represented in your code and that the plan shows no further unexpected changes before applying.

questions.question: You are a mid-level engineer. You notice a Terraform plan shows that an existing AWS RDS instance will be replaced because of a minor parameter group change. You know replacing the database will cause data loss. How do you prevent this while keeping the infrastructure as code?
questions.answer: Use 'terraform state rm' to remove the resource from the state file, then update the code to match the existing RDS configuration exactly. Run 'terraform import' to bring the existing database back under management without triggering a recreation. Finally, verify the plan shows 'no changes' before applying.

questions.question: A Terraform deployment is blocked because an AWS resource has a 'drifted' state. A teammate manually added a tag to a Security Group. How do you resolve this without causing a destructive replacement?
questions.answer: Run 'terraform plan' to see the exact delta. If the drift is just tags or non-destructive properties, update your Terraform configuration to match the manual changes exactly. This brings the state in line without destruction. If the change was truly manual and unauthorized, ensure you have team alignment before 'terraform import' or removing the drift to avoid future conflicts.

questions.question: You are a junior engineer. You need to test if a Terraform script will successfully provision an AWS EC2 instance without actually modifying the production environment. What specific command do you use, and what should you look for in the output?
questions.answer: Use 'terraform plan'. Review the output for the 'Plan: X to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy' summary. Carefully inspect the resource attributes in the output to ensure that tags, AMI IDs, and instance sizes match your requirements. If the plan shows '1 to destroy' or '1 to replace' unexpectedly, stop and investigate the cause before applying.

questions.question: A Terraform plan indicates a change to an AWS Security Group, but you suspect this will break existing production connectivity. How do you safely validate this?
questions.answer: Never apply blindly. Use 'terraform plan -out=tfplan' and 'terraform show -json tfplan' to inspect the specific attributes changing. Compare the current state with the AWS Console or use 'aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules' to identify dependencies. Check the application logs for current traffic patterns. If unsure, update the Terraform code to import the current state or add a lifecycle 'prevent_destroy' block.

questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline using Terraform fails to apply changes because a resource in AWS is locked by an unknown process. How do you safely identify the source of the lock without risking data corruption?
questions.answer: Terraform state locks are managed in the backend (e.g., S3/DynamoDB). Check the DynamoDB table associated with the state file to identify the 'LockID' and the 'Info' field containing the process ID and hostname. Verify if a colleague has a running job, or if it is a stale lock from a previous failed run. Never delete the entry manually without ensuring no Terraform process is actively writing to the state.

questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline fails to run a Terraform plan because the state file is locked. What should you do before attempting to force-unlock the state?
questions.answer: Do not use 'terraform force-unlock' immediately. First, coordinate with the team to ensure no other engineer is actively running a plan or apply. Check the CI/CD dashboard for abandoned or hung pipeline jobs that might still hold the lock. Only after confirming the lock is stale and no process is actually modifying infrastructure, use the command to release the lock to prevent corruption.

questions.question: Your Terraform plan shows that an existing AWS IAM role will be recreated, which would detach it from all EC2 instances. How do you verify the configuration difference and prevent the recreation?
questions.answer: Review the 'terraform plan' output carefully to see the 'forces replacement' indication. Check if the resource name was changed, as Terraform treats name changes as replacements. Use 'terraform show' to inspect the state versus your current code. If the change is necessary, use the 'lifecycle' block with 'prevent_destroy = true' in your code, or move the resource to a separate state file/module to prevent accidental modifications during standa…

questions.question: A Terraform apply fails because a resource (e.g., an S3 bucket) is marked as already existing in the state, but it was manually deleted in AWS. How do you safely synchronize the state without manual editing?
questions.answer: Do not edit the state file directly. First, run 'terraform plan' to confirm the drift. Use 'terraform import <resource_type>.<resource_name> <resource_id>' to re-map the existing AWS resource into the state, or if the resource is truly gone, remove the resource block from the Terraform code and run 'terraform apply' to reconcile the state. Always run 'terraform plan' again to verify the state matches the reality.

questions.question: A Terraform plan reports a change that will destroy and recreate an RDS database. How do you identify which specific attribute change is triggering this destructive action?
questions.answer: Run 'terraform plan' and inspect the output. Terraform explicitly labels destructive changes with a '-' and will note '# forces replacement'. Review the plan output to identify the attribute being modified. Compare the current Terraform code against the AWS Console settings to ensure the change is intentional before proceeding.

questions.question: A mid-level engineer observes that a Terraform plan shows a database instance will be 'replaced' instead of 'updated' due to an attribute change. How do you identify which specific attribute is causing the forced replacement?
questions.answer: Run 'terraform plan -out=tfplan' followed by 'terraform show -json tfplan | jq' to inspect the plan structure. Look for the 'resource_changes' block and check for a field named 'requires_replace'. This explicitly lists the attributes triggering the destruction. Reviewing this before applying prevents accidental data loss; if the attribute is critical, consider using 'lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }' in the resource block.

questions.question: A teammate's Terraform apply keeps failing with 'Error acquiring the state lock' even though no one else is running Terraform. They ran it earlier and it crashed midway. How do you diagnose and safely resolve the stuck lock?
questions.answer: The earlier crashed run left a stale lock in the DynamoDB/backend lock table. First confirm no active apply is running elsewhere. Then use terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> with the ID shown in the error. Never force-unlock while a real apply is in progress, as it can corrupt state. After unlocking, run terraform plan to verify state integrity before applying again.

questions.question: Your Terraform code needs to create S3 buckets for three environments (dev, staging, prod) with identical config but different names. Right now you've copy-pasted the resource block three times. How would you make this DRY?
questions.answer: Use a single resource with for_each over a set/map of environment names, e.g. for_each = toset(["dev","staging","prod"]) and reference each.key in the bucket name. This creates all buckets from one block, keyed by environment, so changes apply consistently. For per-env differences, use a map of objects. Avoid count here since for_each gives stable, name-based addressing.

questions.question: Your team wants to safely test infrastructure changes before applying to production. Currently everyone runs 'terraform apply' directly against prod state, and a bad change once caused an outage. How would you introduce a safer workflow?
questions.answer: Separate state per environment (workspaces or separate backends/dirs). Enforce a plan-review workflow: run 'terraform plan' in CI on PRs and require approval before apply.
